title: Can't Take My Eyes off You
description: Frankie Valli's soaring solo breakthrough — official RHINO audio (the song predates the music-video era), a hushed crooned verse that explodes into the famous horn-driven chorus.

pops.text: The song was written by Bob Crewe and Bob Gaudio, the Four Seasons' house songwriting team — Gaudio was Valli's own bandmate.
The record sat shelved for about a year because the label feared a Valli solo hit meant the Four Seasons were breaking up — Valli insisted he was never leaving.
It was cut in April 1967 at A&R Studio 2 in New York, with Bob Crewe producing, a young Phil Ramone engineering, and an arrangement by Gaudio and Artie Schroeck.
Valli later called this the first step toward his goal of singing in his natural voice instead of relying on his famous falsetto.
The single was rescued by CKLW in Windsor, Ontario — program director Paul Drew put it into rotation after the producers lobbied him, and listener response forced the label's hand.
It peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, kept out of the top spot by The Association's 'Windy,' hit No. 1 on Cash Box, and earned a gold record.
Sharp ears can hear a melodic resemblance to the Adagio from Khachaturian's ballet Spartacus woven into the tune.
Lauryn Hill recorded it in 1997 while pregnant with her first child; tucked onto The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill as a hidden track, it still earned a Grammy nomination without ever being a single.

In 2008 NASA used Valli's version as the wake-up song for astronaut Christopher Ferguson aboard shuttle mission STS-126 — and Heath Ledger's bleachers serenade in 10 Things I Hate About You made it a staple for a new generation.

title: A Whiter Shade Of Pale
description: Procol Harum's debut single — a Bach-tinged, Hammond-organ cathedral of a song that became an anthem of the 1967 Summer of Love, in its original promo film.

pops.text: This was Procol Harum's debut single, released 12 May 1967 and recorded the month before at Olympic Studios in London.
Lyricist Keith Reid lifted the title from something he overheard at a party — one guest telling another she had 'turned a whiter shade of pale.'
Reid actually wrote four verses; only two made the record, though the band occasionally performs the third live.

Gary Brooker built the chord progression from Bach's 'Air on the G String' — as heard in a jazzy Jacques Loussier version in a Hamlet cigar TV ad — reconstructing it from memory and getting it happily 'wrong.'
Organist Matthew Fisher's famous solo line adds a second Bach nod, drawing on 'Sleepers Awake,' played on a Hammond organ that gives the track its church-like sweep.
It spent six weeks at No. 1 in the UK, reached No. 5 in the US with almost no promotion, and has sold more than 10 million copies worldwide.
Fisher was originally uncredited as a composer; in 2009 the Law Lords ruled unanimously in his favour, and the song is now credited to Brooker, Fisher and Reid.
The song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998, and in 2009 was reported as the most-played song in public places in the UK over the previous 75 years.
The video you're watching is genuine 1967 footage of the first Procol Harum line-up, restored and upgraded in 2008 by Henry Scott-Irvine for FLY Records.

title: Me and Bobby McGee
description: Janis Joplin's posthumous No. 1 — a wistful, road-worn farewell recorded for her final album Pearl just days before she died; this official video was created for the song's 50th anniversary in 2021.

pops.text: Kris Kristofferson wrote it on a dare from producer Fred Foster, who suggested a song about a studio secretary named Barbara 'Bobbie' McKee — Kristofferson misheard the name as 'McGee.'
Kristofferson modelled the ending's heartbreak on the final scene of Fellini's film La Strada, where a broken man collapses sobbing under the stars.
Roger Miller recorded it first in 1969 and took it to No. 12 on the US country chart — years before it became a rock standard.

The opening lines came to Kristofferson while working as a helicopter pilot ferrying oil workers in the Gulf: stuck in a Baton Rouge rainstorm, the rhythm of the windshield wipers gave him the song's pulse.
Joplin cut her version between September 5 and October 1, 1970 at Sunset Sound in Hollywood with producer Paul A. Rothchild — finishing it only days before her death on October 4.
Kristofferson, who had briefly been involved with Joplin, didn't know she'd recorded it; her producer played it for him after her death, and he spent the rest of the day walking Los Angeles in tears.

Released posthumously in January 1971, it topped the Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks from March 20, 1971 — only the second posthumous No. 1 in US chart history, after Otis Redding's 'Dock of the Bay.'
Billboard ranked it the No. 11 song of 1971, and Joplin's recording was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2002.

The song had no official video for 50 years; this one was directed by Colombian artist Sara Serna using handmade collage and cut-outs, released March 20, 2021 — exactly 50 years after the single hit No. 1.

title: Dancing in the Moonlight
description: King Harvest's one blissful hit — official audio from the band's own channel (no contemporary video exists), a warm keyboard-led celebration that hides a surprisingly dark origin story.

pops.text: The song was written in 1969 by Sherman Kelly, years before King Harvest made it famous.
Kelly wrote it while recovering from a brutal gang assault on a beach in St. Croix that left him hospitalised — he deliberately imagined the opposite: a peaceful, joyful celebration of life.
Kelly first recorded it in 1970 with his own band Boffalongo, on their album Beyond Your Head; it went nowhere nationally.
The song reached King Harvest through family: Sherman's brother Wells Kelly was drumming for the band in Paris and brought his brother's tune with him.
King Harvest had formed in 1969 at Cornell University, split, then re-formed as expatriates in Paris — and took their name from The Band's song 'King Harvest (Has Surely Come).'
Their version is built around a bright, bouncing keyboard countermelody, with Dave 'Doc' Robinson singing lead.
The single sat unreleased for about a year until Perception Records bought it for worldwide release — it then peaked at No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1973 and No. 5 in Canada.
It remained the band's only real hit — the follow-up, 'A Little Bit Like Magic,' stalled at No. 91, cementing their one-hit-wonder status.
The song got a second life in 2000 when English band Toploader's cover became a worldwide hit and went multi-platinum in the UK.

title: Long Train Runnin'
description: The Doobie Brothers' unstoppable boogie-rock staple — official remastered audio (no video was made in 1973), three years a wordless bar-band jam before producer Ted Templeman insisted it become a song.

pops.text: For about three years this wasn't a song at all — just an untitled, mostly improvised jam the Doobies stretched out onstage, with Tom Johnston making up nonsense words each night.
On set lists the jam rotated through joke working titles, including 'Osborn,' 'Parliament' and 'Rosie Pig Moseley.'
Johnston considered it a throwaway bar tune with no merit; producer Ted Templeman heard a hit, told him it sounded like a train, and ordered him to write lyrics.
Johnston wrote those lyrics at the last minute sitting in the studio bathroom at Warner Bros.' Amigo Studios, because he liked the natural reverb in there.
Johnston sings lead, plays the propulsive rhythm guitar and the harmonica solo; the band's twin-drummer setup — John Hartman plus Michael Hossack on congas and timbales — drives the groove.
Released March 28, 1973 as the lead single from The Captain and Me, it peaked at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Johnston grew up around the rail lines of California's Central Valley, which is why real lines like the Illinois Central get name-checked in the lyric.
It was covered by Italian band Traks in 1982 and by Bananarama in 1991 — then in 1993 a dance remix of the Doobies' own version hit No. 7 in the UK, the band's only UK Top 10 single.
The song's afterlife is so central to the band that Johnston and Pat Simmons titled their official 2022 band biography Long Train Runnin': Our Story of The Doobie Brothers.

title: Let My Love Open The Door
description: The Who's Pete Townshend goes bright, synth-pop solo with a short, joyful plea about divine love that became the biggest hit of his solo career.

pops.text: This is from Empty Glass (1980), Townshend's third solo album — the first built from songs he'd kept for himself instead of giving to The Who.
Townshend has said he meant it as a song about God's love being there in hard times, and in his Anthology liner notes he summed it up in two words: 'Jesus sings.'
His own manager hated it at first because it 'didn't sound like Townshend' and wanted it cut from the album — then called to apologize once it was a hit.
Producer Chris Thomas kept it lean and keyboard-driven, with Townshend himself on guitar and synths, Simon Phillips on drums, Tony Butler on bass, and John 'Rabbit' Bundrick on keyboards.
It was the debut US single from Empty Glass but only the second single in Britain, where it stalled at No. 46 — America got it immediately.
In the US it peaked at No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 5 in Canada, making it Townshend's only solo Top 10 hit in America.
That No. 9 peak exactly matched The Who's biggest US single, 'I Can See for Miles,' which Townshend also wrote 13 years earlier.
Townshend himself was dismissive of it, telling Rolling Stone it was 'just a ditty' — not, in his view, one of his best songs.

In 1996 he reworked it as the slowed-down 'E. Cola Mix' ballad, and the song became a movie-trailer staple in Look Who's Talking, Mr. Deeds, Along Came Polly, Dan in Real Life, and The Adam Project (2022).

title: Let It Whip
description: A Cleveland funk crew on Motown builds an irresistible synth-funk groove out of early drum machines — official audio (no official music video exists) — and dances it all the way to No. 1 and a Grammy.

pops.text: 'Dazz' is a mash-up of 'danceable jazz' — the Cleveland group started as Kinsman Dazz, named for the Kinsman Grill where they were the house band, before shortening it when they signed to Motown in 1980.
The song was written by producer Reggie Andrews with drummer Leon 'Ndugu' Chancler, who said the goal was simple: make a song people could invent a dance to.
It's early-80s technology in action — Andrews and Chancler built the track around a Roland TR-808, a LinnDrum, and a Minimoog bass line, then layered the live band on top.
Released February 12, 1982 as the lead single from Keep It Live, recorded the previous July — it was the group's third Motown album.
It spent five non-consecutive weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's R&B / Hot Soul Singles chart in spring 1982.
It crossed over hard: No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 2 on the Dance chart, finishing at No. 24 on Billboard's 1982 year-end Hot 100.
At the 1983 Grammys it won Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals — in a rare tie with Earth, Wind & Fire's 'Wanna Be with You.'
That win made the Dazz Band the first R&B group from Cleveland to bring home a Grammy.
It keeps coming back — covered by Matt Bianco and Australia's CDB in the 90s, and blasted back into pop culture by the Treblemakers' performance in Pitch Perfect (2012).

title: Why Can't This Be Love
description: A new singer, a keyboard riff that sounds like a guitar, and a huge gamble — Van Halen's first single with Sammy Hagar proves 'Van Hagar' can top the charts; the official video is a live performance, as the band shot no studio promos for 5150.

pops.text: This was Van Halen's first-ever single with Sammy Hagar, who replaced founding frontman David Lee Roth — the whole 'Roth vs. Hagar' era starts with this song.
Warner Bros. actually suggested the band change its name for the new era, floating 'Van Hagar' — the band refused and kept the Van Halen name.
The album title 5150 is double-coded: it's the California police code for a mentally unstable person, and the name of Eddie Van Halen's home studio where the record was made.

In peak MTV era, the band refused to shoot music videos for 5150 at all, wanting Hagar and the music to speak for themselves — which is why the official video for this song is a live performance clip.
Hagar has said the doubters were won over by that opening riff — it was played on keyboards but hit like a guitar riff, unlike the obvious synth sound of 'Jump.'
On the 5150 and OU812 tours, Eddie played those keyboard parts live on a keytar-style controller MIDI-wired to an Oberheim OB-8 hidden backstage, while Hagar played the guitar parts and solo.
It peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 1 on the Cash Box Top 100 and No. 1 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart, and was a Top 10 hit in the UK, Australia, and Germany.
It helped push 5150 to No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — Van Halen's first No. 1 album, later certified six-times platinum.

Its circular lyric 'only time will tell if we stand the test of time' is so famously tautological that The Daily Telegraph put it on a list of the worst lyrics of all time — and Hagar still sang the song at Van Halen's 2007 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction.

title: Blame It on the Rain
description: A Diane Warren ballad built for American radio becomes Milli Vanilli's third straight No. 1 — a year before the lip-sync scandal took everything back.

pops.text: Songwriter Diane Warren didn't write this for Milli Vanilli at all — she wrote it for family group The Jets, who turned it down.
Arista boss Clive Davis rescued it, insisting Warren's song be one of the new tracks added for Milli Vanilli's American album — it never appeared on their European debut All or Nothing.
The voices on the record are not Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan in the video — the actual lead singers were studio vocalists Brad Howell and John Davis.
Producer Frank Farian built it at a slow 98 BPM around a sparse bass line and heavy handclaps — a ballad tempo dressed up as dance-pop.
Listen for the staircase: the verses sit in B-flat major, the chorus steps up a half-step to B major, and the final chorus steps up again to C major.
It debuted at No. 65 on October 7, 1989 and took just seven weeks to hit No. 1, holding the top spot for two weeks starting November 25.
It knocked another Diane Warren song out of No. 1 — Bad English's 'When I See You Smile' — making Warren the only songwriter to replace herself at No. 1 with two such different acts.
It was Milli Vanilli's third and final No. 1, and a Top 10 hit across Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and Europe — but it flopped in the UK, peaking at just No. 52.

A second, longer version of the video exists with a brass-synth intro not on the album or single — and within a year of this topping the chart, the duo's Best New Artist Grammy was revoked when the lip-sync deception was exposed.

title: How Bizarre
description: From one of Auckland's poorest suburbs to No. 1 in five countries — Pauly Fuemana cruises a red Chevy Impala through the strangest, catchiest pop-rap hit New Zealand ever exported.

pops.text: OMC stands for Otara Millionaires Club — a joke name, because Ōtara in South Auckland, where Pauly Fuemana grew up, was one of New Zealand's poorest suburbs.
After the original group split, OMC became essentially two people: Fuemana as the face and voice, and producer Alan Jansson co-writing and building every track in the studio.
The sound is the hook — mariachi-style trumpets and Spanish guitar wrapped around Fuemana's gentle rap and singer Sina Saipaia's 'making me crazy' chorus vocal.
It was an instant smash at home before there was even a video, hitting No. 1 in New Zealand in early 1996 for three weeks and selling over 35,000 copies there.

Director Lee Baker shot the video for just $7,000 of NZ On Air money, on a Ponsonby soundstage and at Ellerslie Racecourse, with Fuemana driving a 1968 Chevrolet Impala, throwing money around, and breathing fire.
Watch the passenger seat: backing singer Sina Saipaia rides along, while Gil Manaois stands in for group member Brother Pele — the video was shown roughly 15,000 times on US networks in 1997–98.
It topped the charts in five countries — New Zealand, Australia (five weeks at No. 1), Austria, Canada, and Ireland — and reached No. 5 in the UK.

In America it never charted on the Hot 100 at all, because it was never sold as a commercial single there and old chart rules barred airplay-only songs — yet it still hit No. 4 on Hot 100 Airplay and No. 1 on Pop Airplay, making OMC the first New Zealand act ever to top a Billboard chart.
It won Single of the Year at the 1996 New Zealand Music Awards, sold an estimated three to four million copies worldwide, and re-entered the NZ chart in February 2010 after Fuemana's death at age 40.

title: Steal My Sunshine
description: Canadian siblings Marc and Sharon Costanzo trade vocals over a looped disco sample in this slacker summer anthem from You Can't Stop the Bum Rush.

pops.text: The whole groove is built around a looped bridge from Andrea True Connection's 1976 disco hit 'More, More, More' — writer Gregg Diamond got a co-writing credit.
Marc Costanzo started writing it after an outdoor rave, sitting far from the stage at 3 a.m. looking at the stars while everyone danced.
Marc and Sharon are brother and sister — and they recorded their sunny duet during a stretch when they hadn't been speaking for months.
Marc modeled the back-and-forth male/female vocal structure on The Human League's 'Don't You Want Me.'
It was recorded in 1996 on a vintage early-1980s 8-track recorder, then almost shelved — the master sat under Marc's bed for months because the band wasn't impressed.
The public heard it first on the soundtrack to the 1999 film Go on March 30, 1999 — nearly three months before it became a single on June 22.
It peaked at No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 3 in Canada, and No. 8 in the UK, with Top 10 placings in Australia and Ireland too.

Marc co-directed the video himself in Daytona Beach during spring break with a $100,000 budget, no script or storyboard — just friends on scooters, go-karts and jet skis, shooting afternoons after sleeping off hangovers.

The video swept the 1999 MuchMusic Video Awards — Best Video, Best Pop Video and Favourite Canadian Video — and the song is now RIAA Platinum and ranked by Rolling Stone among the best summer songs of all time.

title: Young Folks
description: Swedish indie trio's whistled breakthrough duet with Victoria Bergsman from Writer's Block, paired with a charming animated video.

pops.text: That famous whistle was never meant to stay — Björn Yttling whistled it as a placeholder for an organ or other instrument, ran it through tape delay, and the band decided to keep it.
Yttling first imagined the melody as a jazz piano piece that reminded him of Duke Ellington, before playing it on guitar turned it into a pop song.
The band nearly split up before Writer's Block — they agreed to make one more low-budget record in Yttling's small Stockholm studio or quit.

There are almost no cymbals because the room was too small — John Eriksson built a minimalist beat inspired by Daft Punk's 'Robot Rock,' plus bongos, boots on a laminated floor through spring reverb, and tubular bells.
Guest singer Victoria Bergsman of The Concretes couldn't sing it in the original key, so the band pitched the whole track up — which made the whistle even higher and harder to sing live.
Despite the title, Peter Morén says it's not about young people — it's about two burnt-out, jaded people meeting in a bar and cautiously trying to connect.

The animated video was directed by Ted Malmros with animation by Graham Samuels, opening with animated Peter teaching Victoria to whistle on a park bench before a bus ride and a party where everyone disappears.
It first charted at No. 33 in the UK in 2006, then a 2007 re-release climbed to No. 13 — Pitchfork ranked it No. 5 track of 2006 and NME voted it No. 2 Track of the Year.

Kanye West sampled it for his 2007 mixtape Can't Tell Me Nothing and later performed it with the band, while the song went on to the Gossip Girl pilot, FIFA 08, and Platinum certification in the US and UK.

title: Safe and Sound
description: LA duo Ryan Merchant and Sebu Simonian's trumpet-laced synth-pop breakout from In a Tidal Wave of Mystery, about holding on through chaos.

pops.text: Merchant and Simonian met via a Craigslist ad for production services and spent three years writing advertising jingles together before forming Capital Cities.
The song was first released January 6, 2011 on their debut EP, a full two years before it became the lead single for their debut album in 2013.
That signature trumpet line almost didn't exist — it was only added after eight previous versions of the song.
The track is written entirely in C major at 116–120 beats per minute, which helps give it that relentlessly bright, buoyant feel.
There are actually three videos — the first, self-edited by the band in February 2011, intercut a century of historical dance footage with war footage in chronological order.

The famous third video, directed by Grady Hall and shot in the historic Los Angeles Theatre, has dancers from different eras — 1940s swing, 1970s roller-disco, 1990s hip-hop — stepping out of photos and film clips for dance-offs.
The video was nominated for Best Music Video at the 56th Grammy Awards and won Best Visual Effects at the 2013 MTV Video Music Awards, with a nomination for Best Art Direction.

Its chart breakthrough started in Germany after use in a Vodafone commercial, where it hit No. 1 — in the US it finally peaked at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in September 2013, over two-and-a-half years after release.

It kept spreading through covers and ads — Team Adam performed it on The Voice in 2013, and Zendaya, Kina Grannis, Kurt Hugo Schneider and Max Schneider covered it for Coca-Cola in 2014 using Coke bottles as instruments. It is now 6× Platinum in the US.

title: Something Just Like This
description: EDM duo The Chainsmokers team with Chris Martin and Coldplay for a superhero-themed love song about wanting ordinary, real love instead of superpowers — note: this is the official lyric video, as no narrative music video was made.

pops.text: The collaboration was teased in September 2016 when The Chainsmokers posted three short clips featuring Chris Martin's vocal.
On release day, February 22, 2017, Spotify prematurely posted a banner with a 'Listen Now' button at the top of its homepage.
Coldplay and The Chainsmokers premiered it live as a surprise at the BRIT Awards at London's O2 Arena that same day, February 22, 2017.
The lyric video, directed by James Zwadlo and released the same day on Chainsmokers' Vevo channel, uses comic-book superhero illustrations to match the lyrics.
The lyrics name-check Achilles, Hercules, Spider-Man and Batman — the singer admits he has none of their gifts and just wants something real.
Musically it's in B minor at 103 bpm, built on a simple chord loop with Martin's vocal spanning two octaves.
It reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 2 in the UK and Australia, and Top 10 in over 30 countries, spending 39 weeks on the Hot 100.
The lyric video broke the all-time record for a lyric video with over 9 million views in its first 24 hours, beating Justin Bieber's 'What Do You Mean?', and has since passed 2.5 billion views.
It was nominated for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance at the 60th Grammy Awards, set a record with 79 weeks atop Billboard's Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart, and is now 13× Platinum in the US.

title: And It's Still Alright
description: Quiet, galloping-guitar title track from Rateliff's first solo album in seven years, written as a tribute to his late friend and producer Richard Swift.

pops.text: This was Rateliff's first solo album in seven years — since 2013's Falling Faster Than You Can Run — released on Stax Records on Valentine's Day, February 14, 2020, away from his Night Sweats band.
The title track is directly about producer Richard Swift, who produced both Night Sweats studio albums and died in July 2018 after complications from alcohol addiction.
Rateliff had planned to make this solo record with Swift — they envisioned it like a Harry Nilsson record, inspired by Nilsson Sings Newman — and the album is dedicated to Swift.
The album began during a difficult period that also included the end of Rateliff's 11-year marriage, first surfacing in the song 'What a Drag' written at a 2017 Tucson writing retreat.

Much of it was recorded at Swift's own National Freedom studio in Cottage Grove, Oregon, even in his absence, with additional work in Colorado, produced by Rateliff with Night Sweats drummer Patrick Meese and James Barone.
Rateliff said the title song's structure came partly from seeing Tom Petty live with Swift — a friend later joked it was 'only bridges, there's no chorus,' just hook after hook.

The official video was directed by Rett Rogers — who also did the album photography and design — in a grainy film style, mostly black-and-white with washed-out colour, matching the sparse voice-and-guitar arrangement.
The album reached No. 78 on the Billboard 200 and No. 5 on Billboard's Top Rock Albums, with a Metacritic score of 68 from 11 reviews.
Rolling Stone described the album as music pulling Rateliff through his pain toward solace — the title phrase itself is the point: grief and loss, and it's still alright.
